blocks.text: A capacitor is a device that can store electrical energy in the form of an electric field. Two such devices are discussed here: isolated spherical conductors and parallel-plate capacitors (16.5).
A spherical conductor far from other conductors or influences is an isolated spherical conductor. Its ability to store electric charge is called its capacitance, C.

blocks.title: Capacitance of an isolated sphere
blocks.text: The capacitance of an isolated spherical conductor is the charge stored on the sphere per unit electric potential at its surface: C = Q/V (16.25). The SI unit is the farad (F): 1 F is the capacitance of a sphere that stores 1 coulomb when its potential is 1 volt (1 F = 1 C / 1 V).

blocks.alt: A sphere of radius R with + signs all round just inside its surface. Q is marked at the centre, a radius R is drawn to a point on the surface, and that point is labelled V.
blocks.caption: Figure 16.5: Charged isolated spherical conductor of radius R (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 16.5).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 16.5 shows + charges throughout the sphere. On a conductor the charge lies on the outer surface, as drawn above.

The potential at the surface of a sphere of radius R carrying charge Q is V = (1/4 pi eo) Q / R. Substituting in C = Q/V gives C = 4 pi eo R (16.26). In a medium of dielectric constant er, C = 4 pi eo er R (16.27). So the capacitance of a spherical conductor does not depend on the charge or the potential; it depends only on the radius and the medium. A larger sphere stores more charge at the same surface potential, and a dielectric medium increases the capacitance.
